speechtext:
That this House condemn the Government for its negligence with regard to the illegal importation and sale of fuel tainted with polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and other toxic substances.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I cannot say I am happy to have an opportunity to debate this issue but I think it is going to give us an opportunity to put some facts on the record, facts which unfortunately have been in the possession of the Government for some time, up to 28 months, and have been ignored. These are facts that involve a potential risk to the health of Canadians, including the possibility of cancer-causing PCBs being mixed into gasoline fuel, into home heating fuel, into fuel used in industry, into fuel that is used in greenhouses to grow vegetables and fruit which eventually find their way to our tables, leading to the possibility of toxic wastes invading the food chain and posing a risk to the health of Canadians.
I think the first question Canadians have to ask themselves is why, when on several occasions information came to various Ministers of this Government about the possibility of a wide ranging criminal scam, the extent of which we probably have not seen in any kind of trafficking in this country, there has been widespread potential trafficking in toxic wastes between Canada and the United States? When Minister after Minister and Government official after Government official were
informed, why did they sweep the issue under the table? Why did they not want to deal with an issue that could very directly affect the health of Canadians?
I would like to go back for a moment with a bit of chronology. The chronology, if we take it in reverse order of occurrence, would go as follows: In March, 1989, there was a major conference in Switzerland to which the Government of Canada sent the Associate Minister of Transport as its major representative. At that particular conference, the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) was specifically told by Daniel Green-

-the president of Montreal's Society to Conquer Pollution-

-that he had a meeting specifically with Mrs. Martin in which he laid certain facts on the table. To quote Mr. Green, prior to the specific meeting with the Minister of State for Transport, he contacted the office of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard).
I will just read into the record, Mr. Speaker, for the attention of the Government, the names of the people that Mr. Green says he spoke with directly on this issue. In terms of Ministers, he spoke to the Minister of State for Transport. He also spoke to two representatives in the office of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard). He stated this morning, Vic Shantora and John Myslicki. He spoke to Alan Beasley from External Affairs and he also spoke directly to the assistant to the Associate Minister for Transport, Shirley Wood. So we have four Government officials in three departments along with the Minister of State who were specifically told in March of this year about the existence of that scam.
However, that was not the first time that the private sector had tried to alert the Government to the possibility of a major wide-ranging scam which is not, I must point out-

What possible interest could Jim Conrad have in creating a sensation?
The executive vice-president of the Canadian Petroleum Marketers Association is not interested in sensationalism. He has a product to sell and he wants to make sure that it is a clean, untainted product. He is interested in the revenue scam that took place and was being investigated, but he is also interested specifically in the assurances that he should be able to give to Canadians about the quality of his product. That quality has been compromised because of the complete negligence of this Government, the absolute indifference of the former Minister of National Revenue who in January of 1987 was told point blank that there is activity going on in the area of toxic waste importation from the United States. Yet he chose to do nothing.
The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin), who was told in March of this year by an environmentalist whom the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) himself has called a respected environmentalist, chose to do nothing. The Minister of National Revenue stood in the House yesterday and admitted that in September, 1987, almost two years ago, a high level meeting took place in Toronto at which evidence was brought forward about toxic wastes being mixed into fuels, but he claims that the information dealt only with shipping between states in the United States.
My information, from a police informant whom I am sure the Minister will know because he said that copious notes have been kept of the meetings that were taking place on a twice annual basis, gave direct evidence to the Ministry of Revenue and offered to supply ongoing evidence about the criminal nature of toxic products being put into the waste in 1987 and the Ministry of Revenue declined that offer. If it did not have to do with tax fraud, the Ministry did not want to know about it. It was not concerned about the potential, long term implications of this type of toxin coming into the Canadian environment.
Let us look at the broader question, Mr. Speaker. Why would we see the level of shipping of illegal toxins that we are currently led to believe has been going on for the last number of years? Partly because in the United States, for example California, there are extremely stringent laws concerning the disposal of toxic waste. If a company of source is caught shipping toxic waste which ultimately ends up in some type of illegal activity, it is held responsible. If you are the owner of a small operation that may be dealing with used oils in California

and somehow after you tender out your shipping of toxic fuels it ends up in an illegal dump in the State of California, you would be held criminally responsible.
But American law says that once the toxins leave its borders, the original producer of the toxins can go scot-free. So there is a direct impetus on the basis of existing U.S. legislation for American companies to get their toxic wastes out of the United States. Proper, clean, thorough disposal of toxic waste in the United States costs approximately $1,000 for every container that has to be disposed of.
If in the course of exporting that fuel, which may perhaps be laced with PCBs or with other toxins, it finds itself in an illegal dump, as long as the illegal dump is in Canada there is no problem.
I personally was shocked-and I am sure this will shock a lot of Canadians-to learn from the Environmental Protection Agency of the United States, a Mr. Jim Vincent-not a Liberal set-up, not a spokesperson for Canada; everybody is lying except the Government of Canada-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will go back to what shocked me. This is in relation to the fact that Canada is rapidly becoming, in a legal and illegal fashion, the dumping ground for American toxic waste.
If society, and I speak not only of Canada but of the world, is to address the problem of pollution, toxic waste and the environmental damage that causes, we have to understand that there is a basic principle to which we should adhere and that is that we are responsible for our own garbage. In the United States, there are very strict laws which could lead to criminal convictions against companies that illegally dispose of toxic wastes in the United States but make no such provision inteijurisdic-tionally. Because of that, American companies that want to play it fast and loose, want to make the cheapest bid or get the absolute lowest price for disposing of toxic waste, in some cases hand waste over to fly-by-night haulers who use any means whatsoever, including the illegal mixing of toxins into fuel and industrial oil, to get it out of the country.
At the moment, according to the EPA, we are receiving approximately 120,000 tonnes of toxic waste from the United States per year. We are having enough difficulty looking after the toxic waste we create from our own industrial and residential pollution, but we have become the major dumping ground outside the United States for American industrial waste. If we are going to get into the business of looking after other people's garbage, as we have done with respect to toxic wastes from the United States, then at the very least we owe it to Canadians to have a system in place and a Government in place that will respond to the early warning signals, the early warning signals that the former Minister of National Revenue ignored in 1987.
Later, there were warnings at the September meeting of Ministry of Revenue officials in Tbronto in 1987, warning signals which were ignored. Later warning signals were given to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) at an international conference by someone the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) describes as a respected environmentalist. The final signals were laid at the door of the Minister of the Environment in March of this year when once again Mr. Green let his
views be known and his concerns expressed about the possibility of toxic wastes being imported.
The Environmental Protection Agency in the United States admits that the system in place there for the export of toxic waste is subject to flaws. Once a manifest for toxic waste is drawn up, an acknowledgement of consent letter is written to confirm that the particular shipment has been licensed for export but the manifest which includes the original toxins is never cross-referenced with the letter and no check is made to see if companies have consent to export. The American system that is tougher than the one we have in Canada does not even check to see whether companies that are shipping the stuff out of the country have consent to export. That is one major flaw.
If Hon. Members do not believe me, perhaps they will believe Mr. Jim Vincent of the Enforcement Division of the Environmental Protection Agency in Denver, Colorado. He says that rarely are samples taken to confirm a shipment's contents. Usually, if samples are taken, they are taken by the sending company and sent to the receiving company and it is the receiving company that confirms the contents of the sample. That is a bit like having the fox looking after the henhouse. The sending company and receiving company are the only two parties that actually check to see whether the sample of waste is what it is supposed to be.
If there is to be the importation into Canada of 140,000 tonnes of waste a year from the United States, we must have the systems in place to enforce the regulations. This week the Minister of the Environment rose in the House but made no mention of the fact that throughout the mandate of this Government, under the infamous Nielsen Task Force, Customs and Excise alone had 336 positions eliminated. There cannot be the elimination of 336 jobs without there being some effect on control at the border.
The Minister said he would add 34 person-years to his staff which is currently responsible for enforcing regulations emanating from the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. There are 140 border points across Canada. If we assume that people are not capable of working 24 hours a day, 7 days a week-and most of us cannot do that-we can assume that those 34 positions may possibly, at best, be able to cover 8 or 10 border crossings.

That leaves 130 borders unprotected from the potential for major criminal activity and importation of toxins.

That point was raised several times by Mr. Green in his conversations with the Environment Minister's officials and with the Minister of State for Transport Minister. He said that if the Canadian Government was really concerned about toxic substances, it must at least treat criminals in that field as severely as it does criminal drug traffickers.
We know the Revenue Minister made a big fuss last week about various measures he is taking at the border to control drug movement and trafficking.
Mr. Speaker, PCB traffic affects the health of all Canadians. Nearly all Canadian families are suffering from environmental diseases such as cancer, breathing problems, emphysema and so on. The health of Canadians should also be important. For that reason, I think the least the federal Government could do, as was suggested during the debate on the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, is to make sure PCB and other toxic substance traffickers are treated like criminals.
Mr. Speaker, today's papers say that a major PCB trafficker was fined $100,000. But that's practically nothing compared to the profits that can be made over two years.
Mr. Speaker, if the federal Government really wants to improve the situation, it must be recognized that it has ignored the problem for 28 months- But the issue was raised by members of the public and journalists-thank God we have journalists for that-as well as by industry and environment people. I think the federal Government can at least review our federal legislation which does not treat PCB traffickers like drug traffickers and put in place systems to investigate, from beginning to end, the movement of toxic substances in Canada.

A fundamental question will have to be answered over the next few days and weeks. Do we as Canadians want to become the garbage dump of the United States for toxic products? Do we not create enough toxic products from our own industrial, residential and commercial wastes? Perhaps we do intend to make our mark as a major garbage dump for American toxic wastes. If we are

bringing in 140,000 tonnes of the stuff legally, not including illegal importation of toxic wastes, we had better have in place a system to ensure that that toxic waste is properly disposed of.
As a result of what I have seen this week, which has been a comedy of errors and almost Keystone Cops, like the approach to the disposal of illegal hazardous waste, I do not have a lot of confidence that this Government will be able to deliver on a system which will reassure Canadians that PCBs and the other toxins coming from the United States are being properly disposed of. There is a lot of work for the Government. It would behove the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard), who has said that the environment is his number one priority, as the superminister over the heads of other Ministers to refer the matter to a parliamentary committee so that we can all have some input into the process in typing it up.

Mr. Speaker, we have learned in the last few days that the Government of Canada and the Government of Ontario have focused on tax fraud and tax evasion in relation to the bootlegged oil and gas side of this issue rather than on the public health issue. We need to review the history of the poisoned fuel matter. It has become evident that Environment Canada has known about poisoned fuel in Canada since 1985, and Revenue Canada has known about since September 11, 1987. We know the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) learned of it between March 20 and March 22 of this year when Daniel Green discussed hazardous waste smuggling with the Minister of State for Transport at a meeting on the transportation of dangerous goods in Switzerland. Daniel Green also phoned the office of the Minister of the Environment and asked to speak with the chief of staff. Instead, he spoke with Ann Marie Jean. She is currently employed in the Minister's office as a special assistant.
Between April 11 and April 13 a border blitz took place involving officials of Environment Canada, Revenue Canada, the Ontario Department of the Environment, the Ontario Provincial Police and Ontario Revenue. There was one Environment Canada inspector on site whose mandate was to ensure compliance with the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and the Canada-U.S. Agreement on Transportation of Dangerous Goods. There were no Environment Canada in-

May 12, 1989
Supply
spectors on site to investigate compliance with the Canadian Environmental Protection Act which governs "cradle to grave" PCBs and other toxic substances.
An Environment Canada official, Mr. Shantora, says that this was the only sampling of fuel crossing the border in the past year. It would appear that the focus of the border blitz was tax evasion and not public health. Three hundred and eighty- three trucks were checked, and 113 samples were taken for analysis. The samples are being analysed by the Ontario Government for the presence of PCBs and other toxic substances. On May 8 a Globe and Mail story by Jock Ferguson, backed up by two reporters from The Centre for Investigative Reporting in Washington, D.C. revealed information about hazardous waste smuggling to Canada. The Minister of the Environment said in the House and I quote:
Minister Bradley-will be in a position to gather more facts and lay charges.
It became clear at that very moment that the Minister of the Environment was not taking seriously his responsibilities either under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act or in relation to the transport of toxic and hazardous substances into Canada.
There was also a quote in the same article by Mr. Ferguson:
For several weeks now we have been conducting routine border inspections, together with the Province of Ontario, to ensure compliance with the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act. We intend to get in touch with the oil industry to ensure that Canadians are offered high quality gasoline.
That was the line being taken by the Minister of the Environment. By May 9, we found that Daniel Green had revealed his warnings to the Department of the Environment, and the Minister of the Environment said in the House that an official was told in Switzerland, and that the information was passed on to the Ontario Government, which action prompted the April blitz. I quote:
It was not one of my aides, but a civil servant from the department who received the general information from Mr. Green.
Of course, that is directly contradicted by the information from Daniel Green who has been described by the Minister as an extraordinary and fine individual.
The Government then announced a program to address the issue: Border blitzes, including sampling; tracing the movement of fuel from those dealers mentioned in the Globe and Mail story; contacting U.S. authorities; and working with the Canadian petroleum producers.
However, major questions earlier in the week were never answered by the Government side. Why has no attempt been made to find out whether the fuel which is heating Canadian homes, propelling their cars or sitting in Jerry cans in their carports to go into lawn mowers, or for cleaning paint brushes, was contaminated. Neither the Minister of Environment nor the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) have launched that kind of serious investigation. One can only wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the Minister is suggesting that it is safe to bum fuel contaminated with PCBs.
There is not a toxicologist in the world who does not know that if you bum PCBs in a truck, car, lawn mower, or in anything else, you get incomplete combustion and you get furans and dioxins, which are far more lethal and far more dangerous than PCBs. One ten-thousandth of a gram of dioxin will kill you stone dead. To give you some idea of how small it is, Mr. Speaker, anyone who has vacuumed where there is a ray of sunlight coming through a window and sees those little particles of dust floating in that shaft of sunlight, one of those particles of dust weighs about 1/10,000 of a gram. That is how much dioxin there is coming out of the back end of a vehicle that is incompletely combusting PCBs. It is very, very minute quantities.
We have to ask, is the Minister satisfied that there is no PCB contaminated fuel in any Canadian home? This is the time of year when a lot of oil companies go around and top up people's tanks.
Those tanks then sit in a lot of basements and a lot of warm areas, in many cases improperly ventilated, almost always in the lower portion of a home. Why is the Government not doing at least some spot checks to find out? We heard from Mr. Volpe on CBC this morning that there may be nine million litres, not just of fuel, but nine million litres of contamination in terms of various
May 12, 1989

toxic wastes that may be sitting in Canadians' cars, trucks, homes and fuel tanks at various gas stations and so on. Why is it not being located? Why are those people who are most likely to handle it not being advised of the health dangers that they face if they are pumping gas all day long and getting gasoline and diesel on their hands that may be highly contaminated, and not just with PCBs. I will come to the other toxics in a moment.
The Minister of the Environment then suggests that the April 11 to April 13 blitz was prompted by the environmentalist Daniel Green's warning. Only one Environment Canada inspector was on site. There were no inspectors to ensure compliance with the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the keystone piece of legislation for which the Minister is responsible in this matter. Why are there so few environmental inspectors, Mr. Speaker? There are 77 for the whole of Canada responsible under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. The Budget promises 56 more but we have heard of positions promised before.
Currently, even the City of Ottawa has almost as many people making sure there are no parking violations as the federal Government has to check for environmental infractions in the whole country. There are 66 people who hand out parking tickets just in the City of Ottawa.
We know now that this extremely serious criminal conspiracy has been going on for at least four years. As I mentioned in my opening remarks, Environment Canada has known about poisoned fuel being in Canada since 1985.
What about British Columbia? We have not heard from the Government side. No statement has been released to assure British Columbians about toxic fuel that is apparently coming from California into British Columbia. We have heard no statement from Ministers or from Departments about the Province of Alberta, which apparently has toxic contaminated and poisoned fuel coming from the State of Idaho into Alberta.
We know that in Quebec and Ontario it has been coming principally from the Buffalo area, in the State of New York. We know that for the last five months there
Supply
has been a co-ordinating police strike force in Buffalo investigating what has been going on there.
We hear from the Minister responsible for Revenue Canada in his statement to the House on privilege yesterday morning, that all that there had been as far as he is aware was the September 11, 1987 meeting in Toronto. When the FBI has the Canadian border staked out, wanting to see what is going on, they know with certainty there is an interstate movement of poison fuel. We also know that the investigation was focusing on bootlegged fuel coming into Canada, which was Ontario's apparent chief concern. They were trying to capture those provincial taxes, hundreds of millions of dollars per year over the last four or five years. It goes beyond credibility to think that neither the FBI nor anyone from the co-ordinated strike force, nor anyone from any of the state authorities, nor anyone from the state tax authorities would have come to anyone at any of those Canadian border crossings and said: "Look, you should watch out. We know there is the interstate transfer of poisoned fuel. You should be watching out for it".
I think that defies credulity, Mr. Speaker, and I think that goes to the heart of the problem that Canadians are having with the position being taken by the Government that it simply did not know until Monday. We know Environment Canada knew in 1985. We know that Revenue Canada knew since 1987. We know the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) knew since the March meeting in Switzerland.
How do we deal with it, Mr. Speaker? It is an extremely serious matter. I think going back and forth over the history of the matter is helpful, but there are an awful lot of Canadians who want to know how the Government should deal with this kind of an extremely serious situation.
A few months ago, the Minister of Environment, new to his portfolio, responded to the concerns of residents of Quebec and Ontario regarding the 170,000 tonnes of toxic and hazardous waste being trucked into the two provinces from the United States, and indicated that legislative steps were going to be taken to stop the flow of toxic and hazardous wastes from the U.S. into Canada. The Department of Environment has known for many months that large quantities of toxic and hazardous wastes were coming from the United States. Why were they coming? The reason for that is very obvious.

May 12, 1989
Supply
According to Congressman Synor, who has been on television lately, 250 million tonnes of toxic and hazardous waste were produced last year in the United States. Their landfills are filling very quickly. What has happened is that the cost for storage of contaminated materials at landfills has increased massively.
For example, we know that it costs $1,000 to take a 45 gallon drum of PCBs to a proper land-fill. The cost for dumping at all regular dumps in the northeastern interior of the United States has gone from $10 a tonne to $25 a tonne. Many of our land-fills and dumps in Canada are not properly engineered, not properly regulated and many of them do not even have anyone at a gate. One can simply drive in with a truck and dump whatever one likes, without permit, licence or anything.
The Minister of the Environment will know that a former Minister of the Environment, John Roberts, advised Canadians some years ago that about 80 per cent of toxic and hazardous waste produced in Canada is either improperly or illegally dumped. It is dumped on farmers' fields, in creeks, in unlicensed and unregulated land-fills.
As the toxic and hazardous waste problem in the United States reaches crisis proportions, where are they looking to get rid of the materials? Why have mob figures now come to be attached to the whole issue of contaminated waste in the United States? The reason is obvious. The producers would have to pay $1,000 to have a barrel of PCBs properly disposed of, to be eventually incinerated or sealed in a land-fill. The mob buys it. They do not take it to a secure proper land-fill, they dump it into empty tankers. We know this from the work that has already been done by police forces and investigators in the United States. TTiey then go to a virgin fuel filling station and fill the rest of the tanker with virgin fuel, either diesel, gasoline or home-heating fuel, then truck it into Canada.
We know that there was only one fuel test in the past year at Canada's border. It would be obvious to any of those criminal conspirators that one of the best places to get rid of the stuff is not through an interstate transfer where they could get caught and be chased by the FBI in the United States, but to bring it to the nearest neighbour, Canada, and sell it at bargain basement prices, avoiding taxes. But it puts Canadian health seriously at risk.
The Minister of the Environment knows how serious the problem of contaminants has become in Canada. Canadians from coast to coast are aware that one of the great symbols of Canada, the polar bear, is now at risk from PCB contamination. The young males now walking in the Arctic may be the last breeding population of polar bears left in the Arctic. The Minister of the Environment knows the mobility of a lot of those toxic contaminants. They can move through the atmosphere and then, like many of the toxic and hazardous materials, bio-accumulate and bio-magnify. That means that the very small levels of lindane, PCBs and other contaminants moving through the atmosphere, go into the Arctic because of the climatic conditions there, into the marine system and build up in the shrimp and so on. They build up in the seals. We know that there are very high levels of PCBs in the milk of Inuit mothers.
One would have thought that the sanctity and purity of Canada's Arctic was still there. Canadians are now just awakening to the fact that even our northern most pristine environments are becoming contaminated by the unregulated and illegal dumping and handling of toxic and hazardous materials.
We must deal with the issue as though we are on ground zero. Many people around the planet recognize that this whole issue of contaminates are just as risky for humanity as is the potential of nuclear war and nuclear winter. The insidious movement of toxic, hazardous and contaminated materials into our environment, into our wildlife, into food systems and into our air is ending up back in our bodies. It is setting in play genetic time bombs for our future. We cannot predict how great or serious the cancer risk will be. We know that PCBs cause nerve damage, brain damage and serious skin disorders, but the genetic damage that could be happening in this country right now in relation to these contaminants could be extremely high.
If the mob is buying up drums of PCBs to save producers $1,000 a barrel, it is very likely, if not without doubt, picking up the more dangerous and higher contaminants and doing exactly the same thing with them. That is ground zero.

What about zero tolerance? Why has the Minister of the Environment not done exactly the same thing as one would expect with the drug epidemic? The United States went to zero tolerance in relation to those crossing the border with drugs in their vehicles. Now, in the era of deregulation, when the federal Government has direct responsibility for international truck traffic and interprovincial truck traffic, we see the dawn of deregulation.
How many trucks are coming in with contaminated fuel in their gas tanks? How many tankers are coming in with contaminated fuel in the tanks? There are 170,000 tonnes of licensed toxic and hazardous waste coming from the United States, but we do not even know where it goes once it comes into Canada. We must move precipitously to zero tolerance for the importation of toxic and hazardous materials, whether it is in poison fuels, in trucks or anything else.
We must get our own house in order in terms of toxic and hazardous waste. We have not even dealt with the 2,300 PCB sites here in Canada that require incineration. We have not even dealt with the problem at home, in our Territories or provinces, yet there is this avalanche of hazardous and toxic materials coming from the United States.
The United States must also go to zero tolerance. There is information that Canada has also been shipping poison fuel from Canada back into the United States.
The question of zero discharge is something the Minister of the Environment must adopt as his foremost policy. The Minister has recognized the need to do it in terms of pulp mill effluent, in terms of organo chlorines, dioxins and so on. The Minister must deal seriously with the issue of toxic and hazardous waste by making it clear that toxic and hazardous waste produced at any mill site or industrial site anywhere in Canada stays on the mill site until there is an appropriate means of properly disposing of it. Once those toxic and hazardous wastes leave the site, it opens the door to the criminal conspiracies we are now investigating and the U.S. Congress is investigating. Once the waste is out there, the companies that are set up look for the cheapest possible way to get rid of those materials.

Not too long ago I was at the Love Canal with some Members of the House. The New York public interest group, on its way to the Love Canal to show it to the parliamentary committee, passed the Hudson River, which had been on fire. That is how much toxic and hazardous material is being dumped into some waterways in the United States. Someone driving over a bridge threw a cigarette into the Hudson River and, because there was so much toxic and contaminated waste on the surface of the river, it caught fire.
There is a serious crisis with toxic and hazardous waste. Polar bears all over Canada are facing contamination. The fishery in Prince Rupert harbour is closed because of dioxin contamination. The shellfish, prawns and shrimp cannot even be taken out of what everyone assumes is a pristine marine environment.
There must be zero discharge. The Minister of the Environment has an absolute responsibility to move immediately to require zero discharge and the maintenance of those toxic and hazardous wastes on site. When those wastes leave the site we know, according to a former Minister of the Environment, that 80 per cent of the toxic and hazardous waste created in Canada is either illegally or improperly disposed of.
Yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) said it was fear mongering to talk about the possible health implications of having potentially millions of gallons of toxic and hazardous materials in fuel for cars, lawn mowers, trucks, homes and so on. The Government spent $2.7 million trying to convince Canadians about the impact of the national debt. It is very helpful for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to find $2.7 million for that purpose, but what kind of Government would not take the same steps to publish a health alert to advise Canadians of how best to avoid coming into direct contact with toxic and hazardous materials. We know that in 1985 the Minister of the Environment knew there was PCB contaminated poison fuel in Canada. The Government knew about it four years ago. Steps have been missed all the way along.
We must have zero tolerance. We must face up to the fact that we are at ground zero. We must deal with this issue with a sense of urgency. That is the only way to protect the health of Canadians now and in the future.

May 12, 1989

SUPPORT FOR DEMOCRACY IN PANAMA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, General Manuel Noriega of Panama, a criminal on several counts, has denied the people of Panama the basic democratic right to bring to power their choice of Government. Meanwhile, our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) makes a feeble public statement pertaining to "election fraud" and a "volatile situation" in Panama.
Canada is losing all credibility nationally and internationally as an independent, caring, peace-promoting nation. Through unconscionable budget cut-backs in

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-INSPECTION OF TRUCKS
TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-INSPECTION OF TRUCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, international and inter-provincial trucking are areas of federal jurisdiction. In light of that fact and in light of recent revelations about the transborder shipping of hazardous wastes and dangerous goods, and since the provinces have shown themselves unable or unwilling to inspect adequately inter-provincial and international trucking, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) must immediately carry out his responsibility and implement a program of full inspections of trucks carrying dangerous goods across international and provincial boundaries.
A truck carrying dangerous goods crossing an international or provincial boundary should be inspected to determine whether or not it meets safety and maintenance standards, and to ensure that all federal and provincial taxes have been paid. It should also undergo direct inspection as to the nature of the cargo, whether properly contained and loaded, and a determination as to whether or not the cargo is contaminated with toxic wastes.
Instead of that, we have chaos-13 jurisdictions all dabbling in the situation. There is no standard set of guidelines, rules and regulations. There are no uniform standards. Instead, we have incompetence and negligence which are the order of the day for the Government and the respective Ministers responsible.
May 12, 1989

DEVASTATION CAUSED BY FOREST FIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago almost to the day, I made a statement in this House regarding the devastation caused by forest fires in western Canada which were raging out of control. As I speak it is happening all over again.

PEACE PROCESS IN GUATEMALA-PROTECTION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago four members of the Guatemalan Government in exile, the RUOG, entered Guatemala to participate in the peace process. They were accompanied by a number of Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again parts of the West, primarily in the south, show indications that we may have to endure another summer of incredible drought. Surface moisture at this time is quite adequate but the subsurface moisture is very low.
Yesterday and the day before we had incredibly hot winds. However, it is also true that there is sufficient water, if managed properly.
Well over 50 per cent of the snowfall and the rain is lost in the spring runoff. It is lost for irrigation systems, fishing, and water systems for towns.
With properly built dams this water can produce food, not only for Canada but for the entire world. They can also provide water for the many towns and villages in western Canada.
The point is that irrigation dams are good investments. They can enrich the dry areas of Canada and, indeed, the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the anniversary of the birth of Florence Nightingale, and it is also Nurses' Week in Canada.
I invite Members of the House to pay tribute to the service provided to Canadians by Canada's more than
200,000	professional nurses.
I would also invite my colleagues to respond quickly to the crisis in nursing in Canada today. There are thousands of vacant nursing positions in Canada that cannot be filled. This causes serious problems in health care delivery. Nursing is a strenuous and demanding profession, and people are leaving it because of low wages, unacceptable working conditions, and a lack of opportunity to provide effective, professional input into the delivery of health care.
The Government, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty), must respond quickly to the nursing crisis, providing more resources to improve salaries, working conditions, and provide nurses with an opportunity to share as team members in the health care decision-making process.
Perhaps the most important message from nurses to Canadians today is that we spend too much of the $46.2 billion in the health care budget treating sick people rather than keeping healthy people healthy.
Oral Questions NATO

Mr. Speaker, the possibility of ending the cold war and achieving nuclear disarmament was never greater than it is today. As the Soviet Union makes important proposals for arms reductions with the withdrawal of 500 tactical warheads in Eastern Europe this year, and a further offer to pull out all nuclear arms by 1991, if this is matched by the United States, now is the time for Canada to take a strong stand on this crucial issue.
Canada should join with those NATO allies that favour a nuclear-free future by urging the reduction of short-range missiles in the West.
West Germany has been asking for such steps as the weapons sit on its soil. Certain NATO allies clearly see that this move will bring us closer to an end to the nuclear arms race. The cold war can end and it is imperative that Canada, long recognized as a peacekeeping nation, be instrumental in its demise.
Nuclear weapons could destroy this planet and 800 million lives in 12 hours. Let us not miss this chance to guarantee our survival and banish these weapons from Europe forever.

subtopic: DANGEROUS PRODUCTS
DANGEROUS PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me briefly review the events of the environmental situation this week in Canada.
The Minister of the Environment told the House that he knew nothing about the transportation of toxic waste gas into this country from the United States until Monday. The Minister of State for Transport heard allegations in March and claims she took action. The Minister of National Revenue states that he knew nothing about the shipment of toxic fuels until this week. The Minister of Public Works states that he was at a meeting on January 7, 1987, while he was still Revenue Minister, and that meeting was about the shipment of toxic fuels, but he denies that any allegations were made. The Solicitor General says that he only heard about it this week. The Minister of Health knows absolutely nothing about it, but in his usual style claims he is on top of the issue.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, will the Prime Minister haul in this group of bumbling, incompetent Ministers, get them together, get their story together, and produce a straightforward version for Canadians that we can have in a definitive fashion about who knew what, when, why, and where about this toxic mess?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: TOURISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next week is National Tourism Awareness Week.
Under the direction of the Tourism Industry Association, all across Canada, Canadians who make their living from tourism will be telling their fellow Canadians the facts of tourism and emphasizing that Canada grows with tourism.
The facts of tourism tell of an enormous Canadian success story. They tell the story of an industry which is of vital importance to the Canadian economy.
May 12, 1989

In fact, there are 60,000 tourism businesses in Canada employing 600,000 Canadians, and another 500,000 people who depend on tourism for at least part of their livelihood.
This sector has a record of job creation unmatched by any other industrial sector. In fact, tourism ranks second, right behind the auto industry in terms of job creation.
Tourism in Canada is a $21 billion a year business. Of every dollar spent in Canada on consumer goods and services, 6.7 cents is spent on tourism goods and services.
Tourism is also Canada's second largest export industry. It brings in more than $6 billion from foreign travellers.

The tourist industry extend across Canada and ranks among the first in every province and territory. And its future is as promising as its past, Mr. Speaker. According to the Conference Board of Canada's Institute on tourist resources, unemployment in the tourist industry should grow by 16 per cent through 1992.

In fact, by 1994 we expect to have an increase of 2.1 million foreign visitors a year.
The revenue from the increase in foreign visitors is expected to rise from $6.3 billion in 1987 to $13.6 billion in 1994, which means an extra $1.6 billion in tax revenue and the creation of about 145,000 new, full-time jobs.
This Government is committed to working with the industry and the provinces to ensure the continued growth of the Canadian tourism industry.
Together we organized the Tourism Tomorrow Conference, at which the private sector and the provincial and federal Governments reviewed priorities and strengthened co-operative ties.
We organized the Tburism Marketing Council and we sponsored the most ambitious and thorough study ever done of the American pleasure travel market, and shared the results with the provinces and the private sector.
Routine Proceedings
The Free Trade Agreement with the United States will make travel between our two countries easier. This is important for the tourism industry because Canada's largest tourism customer is the United States.
Tourism is very much a small business industry. Eighty five per cent of the 60,000 businesses in the tourism industry in Canada are small businesses. That is they have annual revenues of less than $2 million and employ fewer than 100 people.
This Government is always mindful of the entrepreneurial basis of the Canadian tourism industry. This is an industry filled with risk takers and solid entrepreneurs. Our commitment to encourage and stimulate entrepreneurship will help the tourism industry grow. As we have seen, Canada does indeed grow with tourism.
I am committed to telling parliamentarians, legislators, business people and all Canadians about the importance of tourism to Canada.
Tourism is an important industry which touches every Canadian. We must encourage and an awareness of the industry's importance and an understanding of its challenges and its rewards.
Let us hope that National Tourism Awareness Week will bring about a greater understanding of this industry and a greater appreciation of its importance to the Canadian economy.
I urge all Members of the House and all Canadians to join me in paying tribute to the men and women of the tourism industry, and to help promote Canadian tourism next week.

I would like to emphasize that the Canadian tourist industry criticized the last Budget, and I would like to quote just one sentence here: Increased costs and reduced marketing expenditures are bad news for the $21 billion Canadian tourist industry. Tourism Canada's international marketing budget will be slashed by a third over the next three years, at a time when there is serious competition internationally for the tourism dollar and its benefits. According to Mr. Rowe, chairman of the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, we have now reached a point where the Americain States individually are spending more than the Canadian Government to promote tourism. To take one example, Mr. Speaker, the State of Illinois is spending more than the Canadian Government on tourism promotion.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of aspects in the tourist industry on which we could focus. It was taken for granted over the years that the tourist industry could go on automatically. This is not the case. The fact is those industries create jobs. They sometimes need to be supported, but they would like above all to be consulted in order to make adjustments. Certainly, if the Minister took the time to consult the various Canadian tourist associations, he could learn a lot of things to improve the situation of the very important Canadian tourist industry.

In conclusion, I bring to the attention of the House the fact that there is a great deal of competition internationally to get tourist dollars. Everyone recognizes that, especially those in the tourist industry. However, when we see that one single state of the United States, the State of Illinois, spends more than the Government of Canada to promote tourism, I think the time has come to review our tourist promotion program and to sit down to
listen to those who make their living from tourism. They are the experts in the field. From what I have seen over the last few weeks, after having consulted with those people they will be only too glad to join with the Government in seeing that their industry is kept alive and vibrant.

Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to thank the Minister of State for Small Business and Tourism (Mr. Hockin) for providing my office and that of my Liberal colleague with an advance copy of his statement. That has given me an opportunity to provide a thoughtful reply to the Minister's comment.
At this time I would also like to join with the Minister in recognition of the tourism industry and its economic benefits to Canada. As the Minister has pointed out, the tourism industry is an important component of Canada's national economy. I hope that the importance of this industry will be highlighted next week during the celebration of National Tourism Awareness Week.
Tourism is Canada's fastest growing industry. In every province it has ranked first in the creation of new jobs, most of them in the small business sector. There is virtually no other industry which contributes more to Canada's regional development than does the tourism industry. It is already the largest employer in Canada. By the year 2000 it is expected that tourism will be the leading industry in Canada.
The Minister and I are in full agreement that the tourism industry is indeed a vitally important component of our national economy. Yet I am concerned that despite the good intentions of the Minister of State for Tourism, his colleagues in Cabinet have failed to understand the current and future economic impact that this industry will have in Canada.
It is evident in the legislation currently before the House that the Government wants to relegate tourism to the back-burner of economic development by hiding it within the proposed Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology. The Government has not given my colleague the status of a full ministry, something that the industry has been calling for over some time. I am sure that the Minister is reluctant to bite the hand that feeds him so I will come to his defence and say this to his colleagues on the Government side of the House: It is time that the Ministry of Tourism be given the priority
May 12, 1989

and profile it needs and deserves in order to do its job properly.
Maintaining the Department of Tourism as a sub-ministry fails to acknowledge the growing importance of this industry in Canada. It fails to recognize the commitment that the Government made back in 1984 to increase the profile of the Department.
Since that time we have seen member after member of the Government praise the importance of the tourism industry. The industry itself has made it very clear that it is not satisfied with anything less than a full-fledged ministry. It has called repeatedly for the establishment of a separate Ministry of Tourism with a status equal to other major economic sectors. The Government has continued to ignore such appeals. Whether we can meet the expectations of the market-place in the future will be critical in terms of Canada becoming globally competitive in the tourism industry.
Although it is indeed a growth industry in Canada, our international tourism deficit has grown steadily. We have reached an all-time high in our tourism trade deficit of about $5.2 billion. To remain globally competitive, we will have to do better. We will have to develop and be more aggressive in marketing our tourism product. That will take initiatives that can be developed only through a full-fledged Ministry of Tourism, not a miniscule Department that is hidden within the bowels of another ministry. It will take a commitment from the Government to put its money where its mouth is, to assist the industry in the task of international marketing.
Over the past 10 years, federal investment in tourism marketing has not even kept pace with inflation. We have now reached the point at which some individual states in the United States, as my Liberal colleague pointed out, spend as much on tourism marketing as does the entire federal Government.
According to the spending estimates, the average expenditures for tourism development have not even kept pace with inflation. That is not enough for an industry poised to become the largest industry worldwide by the 21st Century. Yet what has been the
Routine Proceedings
response of Government? It has slashed $10 million- fully one-third of its foreign marketing budget.
I am certain that my colleague, the Minister of State for Tourism, is genuine in his commitment to the industry. However, we are going to need more than the soothing words of the Minister if Canada is to become a competitive player in the global market-place of tourism.
I welcome the opportunity to work together with my colleague, the Minister of State for Tourism, to ensure that the concerns of the tourism industry are both heard and acted upon by the Government.

speechtext:
As you know, Mr. Speaker, with your great experience, it is often difficult here to keep perspective on things spoken of in the House. I believe that I can put a better perspective on some matters spoken about by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) before we broke for Question Period.
Yesterday the Hon. Member spoke about this PCB-contaminated material touching a person's hand as he was filling his lawn mower or his car. Today he spoke about the polar bears being at risk from PCBs.
I wish to relate a story about this issue. A major environmental scientist spoke to me about what he would do if he were working in a laboratory and there was a container with a high concentration of PCBs in that lab and he dropped his pen into that container. Would he give up his pen? Would he walk away from it? Would he put on a glove and reach into the container? This scientist stated that he would simply reach into this container with his hand, pull out his pen, wash his hands off, and not think anything more about it. I asked a

relative of mine the same question. He is also a reputable scientist. He stated that he would do the same thing. I relate this story to indicate that perhaps PCBs in themselves are not as violently toxic as the rhetoric might indicate.
The Hon. Member for Skeena stated that thousands of gallons of contaminated material have been trucked into Canada. This morning we heard that Mr. Conrad is now suggesting that his information was not as positive as it appeared before, and a constituent of mine, Mr. Hammond, who attended those meetings has stated that this was not mentioned in the meetings with the people from Revenue. How can the Member for Skeena be so sure? What proof does he have that the trucking of contaminated fuel is occurring?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - ILLEGAL IMPORTATION AND SALE OF TAINTED FUELS
speechtext:
First, I would like to comment on the Hon. Member's remarks. It is highly irresponsible in the extreme to be suggesting to Canadians watching the proceedings of the House of Commons today that it is quite appropriate to stick your hands into pure PCBs. That is extraordinarily irresponsible. I hope that the Minister will rise and expunge that remark from the record.
It is not only PCBs that we are concerned about here. There are many other serious contaminants associated with this poisoned fuel scam. The Hon. Member should know that. To suggest that it is appropriate to bathe your hands in PCBs and then wash them in the sink and let that go down the drain is the height of irresponsibility. That is why the Government should not continue to be in office.
In terms of proof, Mr. Speaker, one of the chief law enforcement officers in the United States has stated now that in February, 1988, federal officials were advised that the poisoned fuel scam was going on. made reference to it in his letter. But no reference was made in that letter.
Furthermore, on March 13, a few months later, Mr. Conrad sent a telex to the Minister's office pointing out in detail the discussions that took place on January 7 in the Minister's office with Mr. Conrad. In detail-it is a long telex-he pointed out all the things they talked about. Nowhere in the telex from Mr. Conrad to the then Minister dated March 13, 1987, is there any reference whatever in way, shape or form to contaminated fuel, let alone the possibility of contaminated fuel coming into Canada.
We go a little further. On May 20, a very nice day-it happens to be my birthday and I want Hon. Members to remember that because it is coming up soon-Mr. Conrad gave testimony to the Finance and Economic Affairs Committee. It is fairly long testimony on fuel. I did not figure out how many hours but it is hours of testimony filling about 40 to 50 pages. There is not one reference by Mr. Conrad or by anybody else in the committee hearing regarding contaminated fuel, let alone the possibility of contaminated fuel coming into Canada.
Finally, although Mr. Conrad has said that he did talk to the then Minister about this on January 7, it is very strange because we find confusion in Mr. Conrad's statement. I guess all Liberals seem to be confused and it seems he falls into that category. One day he said that he did discuss the matter with the Minister on January 7, and this morning on Canada AM and I quote: "When referring to that meeting with Mr. MacKay, Mr. Conrad said, well, the meeting focused primarily on tax evasion so we didn't deal explicitly with the toxic contamination". "We did not deal explicitly with the toxic contamination", so there you have it, Mr. Speaker. The first time anything came to my attention in a documented way in hard evidence where Mr. Conrad is concerned about contaminated fuel was today when a copy of a letter dated May 11, 1989, arrived.
We have already said that we have been aware of allegations of contaminated fuels since last Monday. This letter dated May 11, 1989, was signed by Mr. Conrad, the executive director of Petroleum Marketers Association of Canada. It is a Dear David letter, the David he is referring to is David Peterson, the Premier of the Province of Ontario. I will not read the whole letter,

May 12, 1989
Supply
but Mr. Conrad states: "Dear David, you know of my strong support for you and the Liberal Government, but you have a serious problem and I would like to offer a constructive suggestion". He goes on to say,
"My frustrations and those of the industry and environmentalists is that your officials in the Province of Ontario, both in the Ministry of Revenue and the Ministry of Environment, have repeatedly stonewalled all suggestions and recommendations from this association. Jim Bradley is only damaging the reputation of Government when he says he has the answers when he doesn't. David, your officials don't have the answers. They are the problem, not the solution.".
This is the first time any hard evidence has come to our attention that Mr. Conrad is really concerned about the environment or about contaminated fuels. We have dug through other files including the files of the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) when he was Minister of National Revenue and talked to the people who were at the meeting with Mr. Conrad and the former Minister of National Revenue, and as the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) would say, not a twitter or twaddle of evidence is there that there was ever an indication by Mr. Conrad to suggest that he was concerned about contaminated fuel, let alone the importation of contaminated fuel into Canada. Let me just say, so much for Mr. Conrad and his allegations.
We are being told that we are not moving fast enough or in a co-ordinated way. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Timer) this morning in Question Period said that Ministers do not talk to each other. He may think that because Members on his front benches do not talk to each other, the same is true on this side. It of course is not true.
As soon as this matter came to our attention through the story in The Globe and Mail on Monday, all appropriate Ministers not only talked to each other but met on a regular basis with officials to bring together a co-ordinated program. In Customs within the Department of National Revenue, immediately upon finding out that there was an indication of a concern, we developed a national sampling program which was implemented on May 10 this year. All Customs operational service
managers have been notified that these inspections will be carried out across Canada.
Canadian importers dealing with these companies have been identified. Lookouts against these companies are now in our automated system and the details of any shipments involving these companies are being immediately sent to Ottawa and shared with the RCMP and the Department of the Environment. A national print-out of all importation of oil and gas products has been forwarded to Environment Canada and is being shared by the various Departments associated with this problem.
Today the Minister made a four point announcement, and the part of it that will affect Customs Canada is the reduction of the number of border points across Canada so that we can direct tanker traffic into certain border points where we can be in a position, in conjunction with the Department of the Environment and the various provinces in utilizing professional customs officers within the Department of National Revenue, to make certain that the best and fullest possible tests on fuel will take place.
At this moment my officials are working on an implementation plan and they will continue to work until that plan is ready. Once that plan is ready, customs officers will be notified. The plan will be implemented and an announcement will be made accordingly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say that the Government does not make a habit of responding to any or every newspaper story that may or may not be factual or may be speculative. We deal with facts. That is number one. The RCMP is investigating this whole matter and that is another situation. I suspect, believe and understand that the RCMP is looking into any allegations that are made in the news media or elsewhere. I am not sure, but I understand that that would be the case.
Inasmuch as we in the Cabinet are concerned, we have to deal with the facts that are made available to us. We have Departments that are run by very professional people who look into the situation in a very clear and succinct way. We follow up on the information that has been given to us in a open and professional manner. We would be in a shambles as are the two opposition Parties, if we had to respond in a quick kneejerk way to any suggestion or any newspaper story that may or may not come up on any given day.
As far as the September 11 meeting is concerned, the Hon. Member asked me a question which I will paraphrase. I think he said: "Is the Minister saying that at no time in that meeting was there any mention in regards to contaminated fuel?" I did not say that there was not a mention in respect to contaminated fuel.
What I said was made very clear on numerous occasions. The meeting came to my attention two days ago. The earliest opportunity for me to respond was yesterday, at the beginning of the sitting of the House at 11 a.m. I rose on a question of privilege and I said that according to our information and our sources who were at the meeting-our officials spoke to all seven people

May 12, 1989
Supply
from Revenue Canada-the meeting was held because of tax evasion concerns with which we were dealing in conjunction with the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec and the U.S. Internal Revenue Department. An informant alluded to the fact that a truck driver in the United States told him some time ago that perhaps there was some questionable material put in his fuel tank for transportation to another state in the United States. I understand and I am led to believe that that is the reason revenue officials at that meeting-there were seven revenue officials, five from Customs and two from Excise-did not report that statement from the informant to higher officials in the Department of Revenue was that there was nothing in that one brief statement or two; I believe he referred to the truck driver twice. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to tty to answer as many questions as possible.
First, on the quantity of custom officers, there is an ongoing effort to try to make better use of officers. It is true that there has been a reallocation of some Custom officers over the past few years. The fact is that there are approximately 3,000 professional Custom officers working on behalf of Customs Canada at every border crossing in the United States. There are times when others are brought in to assist during peak periods of tourist traffic and so on.
What is the co-ordination between Custom officers and environment? Whenever there is a check on toxic substances, whether it be in contaminated fuel or anywhere else, obviously Custom Canada officers must be there to co-operate with environmental officials.
I will repeat what I said earlier. At this moment officials of Revenue Canada, Department of the Environment and other Departments are working together to create a plan which we hope to implement at the earlier opportunity, whereby we will reduce the number of border points for traffic of liquid fuels. At such points there will be both Custom officers and environment officers, hopefully with the co-operation of the provinces as well, to make certain that we will be able to inspect and check as many, if not all, the fuel tankers coming into Canada as possible.
As the Minister of the Environment said earlier, there are never enough resources available. We wish there were more. The number of experts in the Department of the Environment has increased. There is co-operation and co-ordination between the Department of Environment, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Transport, the appropriate Ministers, and the Department of National Revenue. We are currently developing an implementation plan to put teams at those border crossings that we feel are the most appropriate to deal with the situation. That is the action plan we are taking, despite the fact that to date there is still no evidence that contaminated fuel is coming into Canada from the United States. The Minister of the

Environment outlined this morning that the tests taken thus far prove that there was no contamination. We are taking the precaution because we are the responsible Government. We are consistent, and we are dealing with this as effectively and efficiently as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - ILLEGAL IMPORTATION AND SALE OF TAINTED FUELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue being debated today is a very important one. I want to assure the House and Canadians that this Government regards it as seriously as any other Party or any other group of individuals.
A great deal of attention focused during the course of this week on the stories which appeared in The Globe and Mail beginning on Monday. As Parliamentary Secretary I have had the occasion to be present during most of the meetings which have taken place during the week. Clearly the Minister of the Environment stated before the House on numerous occasions that he learned of the allegations only when he read the newspaper account on Monday. A great deal of debate during the course of the week has been focused on what may or may not have occurred rather than on what should be done. We could waste a great deal of energy and time in the House focusing on the past rather than focusing on the future.
If all Members of the House are as concerned about the environment and the health of Canadians as indeed I think they are, then I would suggest that it would be most appropriate for the House to use the time and energy remaining in the debate today and lying ahead to try to address the concerns of Canadians which exist. It would be appropriate to put them in some sort of proper perspective and to ensure that proper procedures are put in place so that we can assure Canadians wherever they may live that they need not fear for their future when they use the petroleum products on which we in Canada so heavily depend.
I would like to take a few moments this afternoon to talk about the petroleum industry because it is a very, very important part of the whole process. Certainly there has been a great deal of discussion about the the role of Governments at both levels and interested individuals. The petroleum industry is one which must be a very integral part of the process. It must be a very valuable partner if we are to make sure that the measures that
Supply
need to be in place are there, and if we are to reassure Canadians as we would wish to do.
To be realistic, I think there is a certain tendency in Canada on frequent occasions to malign industry, particularly if it happens to be big industry. Perhaps we are all somewhat guilty of that. I would suggest that the petroleum industry in Canada has in recent years spent vast sums of money, millions of dollars, upgrading its facilities to ensure that its products are as protective of the environment as they possibly can be.
It has demonstrated its willingness to be part of the process, to confirm the recent announcement of the Minister of Environment that the use of leaded gasoline will be banned by December 1, 1990, a full two years sooner than had originally planned. It has indicated its ability to co-operate with that deadline.
I am certain no one more than that industry has been alarmed by the reports in The Globe and Mail during the course of this week. Certainly anyone who has read them cannot help but be disturbed by them. There have been allegations that tainted fuel has been coming into Canada. Perhaps this is a fact. We have to remember that these are allegations rather than proven facts. There is also the allegation that there are connections with organized crime, which of course alarms us all.
One of the reasons we are so concerned is the fact that any talk of PCBs is alarming to us all, particularly those of us who are lay people and may not even understand the nature of PCBs, let alone what their impact on the environment or on individuals could be.
Earlier this afternoon we heard a debate within a debate about how the science community is reported to have responded to PCBs and about the concerns of other members expressed at those reports.
I am afraid I left my chemistry back in first year university, but what is evident is that it is very difficult to dispose of PCBs. They must be burned with great care. They are very persistent and therefore a tremendous danger to our environment.
When we talk about tainted fuel, we must first of all appreciate the fact-and this has been said here on several different occasions this afternoon-that there is as yet no evidence discovered by the many people who are now part of the process. There has been no evidence found of tainted fuel. As I say that, I do not dispute the allegations in what is obviously a very well researched series of articles in The Globe and Mail this week,

Supply
indicating that there has been a number of investigations, that a number of samples have been taken at the border, and that to date there is no evidence of PCBs being found.
We would perhaps be naive if we were to sort of hang on to that as evidence that there need not be reason for concern. It is important to remember that we are dealing with the fact that the evidence has not yet been found. It may indeed well be found.
The question which the motion before the House addresses, is important. It deals with how the Government has responded to the crisis that has emerged, how the Government has responded to the concerns which have been expressed. I would suggest that the Government has responded exceedingly well this week, bearing in mind that there has not been a lot of hard information, there have been rumours, and there has been fear expressed.
The Ministers within the federal Government immediately began to correlate their activities among themselves. I saw several meetings of Ministers take place this week, those who have a concern-Customs, Revenue Canada, Health, Transport, and Environment. At the same time meetings were set up and contacts were made with counterparts in the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I attended briefly a meeting this morning at which there was a Minister from the Province of Alberta. I know that communication is passing from the federal Government to all other provinces.
In addition, there was a meeting last night between representatives of the petroleum industry and officials from Energy, Mines and Resources, from Environment, from Health and Welfare, and from Customs and Excise, to review what is known and to plan for the future. The emphasis throughout the course of the week has been on the need for government at all levels, the industry, and the interested parties to work together in a co-operative manner in order to plan for the future and to address the reported problems.
If indeed we are considering what is good for the country, what is good for Canadians, and what is in the interest of those who are here and those who are watching on television, I would suggest that the emphasis should be on what is needed to address the possibility of
tainted fuel coming into Canada. It is far more important to plan and work together in co-operation than it is to launch allegations back and forth across the hall, back and forth across the House or on television with respect to who said what to whom at what particular time, or who did not say what to whom at any particular time.
I believe there is a message for us as parliamentarians in the polls, in the sense that public opinion polls have told all of us who are interested in listening that the environment is a very major issue in the minds of Canadians, that there is a great deal of concern of people of all generations.
There is this interest in the environment and this fear for the future. Recently I came back from Helsinki where I attended a follow-up conference to the Montreal Protocol meetings, and it was evident that there were far too many CFCs in the environment than we would wish. What is particularly distressing is that the CFCs which are there will remain there regardless of what we do by way of reduction of emissions for a hundred years.
I think the public is now beginning to tell us as politicians and as parliamentarians that the problems of the environment are far, far too important to be diverted by partisan differences and partisan debate within the House of Commons. If indeed there is an issue before this House which deserves and needs the attention of the House in a non-partisan manner, I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all Members of the House that that issue is the environment.
We may often disagree in terms of what is needed to be done. We may disagree on who is most capable of doing it. However, surely, we should never disagree on the importance and the difficulty of the task which lies ahead. While we can afford our partisan differences, and while perhaps they are a necessary part of the cut and thrust of parliamentary debate, I believe Canadians are telling us pretty loud and clear that they do not want politicians spending an entire day in the House of Commons trying to score political points. What they really want are politicians to work together in order to develop a strategy that will ensure that the gasoline we buy in the pumps when we go home for the weekend, regardless of whether we buy it from an independent or we buy it from one of the major suppliers, is what it is
May 12, 1989

purported to be and that the air we breathe is as free of contaminants as we can conceivably make it.
If we are to achieve that objective, we must keep our partisan considerations at least to a minimum. We certainly would have to be exceedingly naive if we were to assume that they would ever disappear. I see an Hon. Member across the hall who sat with me on the Agriculture Committee in the past. One thing that always pleased me about the Standing Committee on Agriculture was that I think we were essentially as non-partisan in that committee as we could ever be. We recognized that the problems in agriculture did not all originate within Canada. They could not all be blamed on the Government, or government at any level even though there is sometimes a temptation to do that.
If we were really to develop policies to assist the Canadian farming community, we realize that it has to be done in as much of a spirit of non-partisanship as possible. I believe we came admirably close to that objective.
I suggest that members of the Standing Committee on Environment take up the task of examining all the information that is before us this week. That would be a very appropriate challenge for that committee.
I believe the most productive way, for all of us who are sincerely concerned about the environment, to address the issue is to focus on what is needed in the future rather than on what may or may not have occurred in the past.
It is essential that the industry be considered as a partner in that process. That is why I believe it was extremely important that the industry met with officials last night. I hope it has the opportunity to meet with provincial officials as well in the near future. It is important that they have agreed to meet again.
I had the opportunity to attend a meeting this morning. While I sat in the room I did not think about the politics of the people there. It was only after a few moments that I realized that the Minister of the Environment who was chairing the meeting, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and their counterparts from the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec were not of
Supply
the same Party. Of course, that is true for the Minister from the Province of Alberta as well.
The fact that they were not from the same Party was not relevant to the discussions that were taking place. I believe there is a lesson to be learned from the interaction of officials. There is a lesson to be learned from the interaction of Ministers, which all of us in the House of Commons could learn particularly with reference to environmental matters.
Canadians are telling us that this issue is the most important one in Canada today. It is the most important issue for the next decade and perhaps the next century. PCBs last for a long time. CFCs last for five generations. We are talking about a problem that has great significance for Canadians for generations to come. That is why it is essential that we work together to devise a strategy to resolve the problems at hand.
Today the Minister of the Environment dealt with proposals for the future and the possibility of adding more toxic substances to the Hazardous Waste Act. That is why I stress it is important to look to the future and keep our differences to a minimum so we may concentrate on what is needed for the well-being of the country in the years ahead.

speechtext: What would you have done?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - ILLEGAL IMPORTATION AND SALE OF TAINTED FUELS

Let me say that I reflected very carefully on everything that was said to me in Helsinki last week to ensure, quite frankly, that there were no casual conversations of which I was a part and may not have fully understood as a lay person.
