Last week in Helsinki, if I had talked to Dick Buxton, an internationally distinguished expert on CFCs, and he made a contact back to Ottawa to his superiors, I would have assumed, based upon my knowledge of the issue, that he had done the right thing.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - ILLEGAL IMPORTATION AND SALE OF TAINTED FUELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, both the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister earlier this afternoon said that there is absolutely no evidence of any contaminated fuels crossing the border.
I assume that this assertion is being made on the basis of the results thus far from the sampling that was undertaken in a remarkably prescient border blitz from April 11 to April 13, given that the Government claims to have known nothing of this matter prior to last Monday. However, serendipity does work in human affairs.
As I understand it, during this blitz on April 13, 383 trucks were checked from which 113 samples were drawn. Of these some 30 to 35 were samples drawn from fuel trucks.
According to The Globe and Mail this morning the results of the testing of these samples have been received from the Ontario Government for 12 such samples. Certainly, less than half of all the fuel samples taken is a statistically insignificant amount.
I am wondering if the Parliamentary Secretary has some other sampling on which to base his contention that there is no evidence, or if perhaps he has received more samples than have thus far been publicly reported. Perhaps he is jumping the gun just a tad in this instance, rather as the Government did in the matter of the Budget leak, where in the 24 hours immediately following the leak, there was absolutely no question that the leak was but a consequence of theft. There was no question that it was undertaken by a criminal. These are judgments which seem since to be somewhat tempered.
I was wondering if his assurance in this instance might not become similarly tempered over the next little while.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter into the debate. During the past week Members of the House have expressed their concern about the performance of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard). Some have even called for his resignation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has responded by singing the praises of his Ministry and calling on the entire House to support his efforts in protecting our environment and the health of Canadians.
When we look at the record of what has been happening in the Ministry of the Environment, we see the tanker problem on the West Coast. The wildlife there is suffering. The whole environment of the West Coast has been attacked. According to the Ministry, no one could foresee that everything was not safe and all right.
Here we have a situation in the United States where it has been identified that from state to state there is a problem. Both the Ministry of the Environment and the Ministry of National Revenue did not see forward enough to feel that possibly these types of things might be taking place in Canada. That is not acceptable.
The Minister has praised the Environmental Protection Act. I would like to speak about that Act. I wish to look at the administrative duties, especially with regard to what is expected of the Minister. The Act states that the Minister should take both preventive and remedial measures in protecting the environment. He should take the necessary steps to protect the environment while making social and economic decisions. He should endeavour to act in co-operation with the Governments of the provinces to protect the environment, and encourage the participation of people in Canada in making decisions that affect the environment.
He should facilitate the protection of the environment by the people of Canada, and endeavour to establish nationally consistent levels of environmental quality. He should provide information to the people of Canada on the state of the Canadian environment, and apply knowledge, science and technology to resolve environmental problems. He should endeavour to protect the environment from the release of toxic substances, which is what we are talking about here today. He should endeavour to act expediently to assess whether sub-

May 12, 1989
Supply
stances in use in Canada are toxic or capable of becoming toxic.
At the very least the Government should come forward immediately and start to test all greenhouses in Canada. It should take samples from their oil tanks to ensure that there is no toxic material to be found.
At this time of year greenhouses are producing vegetables which will be distributed throughout Canada and planted in our gardens. If the fuel being used is toxic and these young plants are being distributed across Canada and planted in our gardens, then I think the Canadian people should know.
If such a situation has been taking place for two years in the United States and the Government has said it has checked since Monday then, my goodness, once the word is out we cannot expect those oil carriers to cany this toxic fuel into Canada anymore. The Government should at least make some checks across Canada in various areas. It knows where these greenhouses are. The oil tanks in these areas could be easily checked. It would give us some idea that the Government is ready to take some action.
I want to speak for a minute if I may about the Environmental Protection Act. I think it has some very serious loopholes in it. I have in my riding a small community called Elko, British Columbia. The citizens of that community have been subjected for the past three months to one of the most blatant and underhanded uses of the burning of waste chemicals from a pulp mill. The pulp mill is operating under outdated technology which is its right under the Act since it was built before 1971. This company, Crestbrook Forest Industries, is now in the process of trying to establish a new pulp mill in Alberta to the tune of $1.3 billion. At the same time that this is going on, in the small community of Elko it is being allowed to take caustic chemicals from its pulp mill to an open, outdated beehive burner and bum them into the atmosphere.
No one knows the ramifications of this process. For the past year this community has been fighting that process through the waste management branch. It has spent $17,000 of its own money. When a company comes forward with an idea such as this, there are no provisions for the people involved to have some revenue to fight
this big company, and to identify their concerns. What will happen when this chemical comes out of the stack and into the grass and the cattle eat it. This has never been done in North America before, and it is something that is very serious to them.
Early in March I met with people from the Department of the Environment and brought this issue to their attention. To date I have not received a response from that Ministry with regard to the serious problems that could be caused from that type of activity. Elected representatives from the State of Montana, approximately 20 kilometres away, object to this process. The residents in the community object to it. The Ministry has not even shown the courtesy of conducting a simple test to assure the people that they are protected, or that there are serious problems concerned with it.
Because of the fight by the residents of Elko, and because of the representation we have made, with support from the State of Montana and the people backing us there and the workers in the mill, the company has decided to withdraw and quit. However, it was not because of the efforts of the Ministry of the Environment. It was because of the efforts of those individuals who put forth their own money, time, and effort to ensure that their environment was protected.
We have a very serious problem. We have a Minister who talks about the environment, but does very little about protecting it. When we are faced with even the possibility of poisonous materials mixed in with gasoline and fuel oils, the people of Canada deserve to know that the Government would go back two, three, or six months to check that fuel in various areas of Canada to ensure that it is clean. If it is not clean, then definitely the Department should do some checking as to the effects of those plants on the environment, or the people involved with it. It is a very serious matter, and one that we must deal with, and deal with now.
Members of the Government state that members of the Opposition do nothing but oppose. We have called for an all-committee investigation of this matter, but the Government does not want an all-committee investigation. It knows if members of the two opposition Parties become involved the truth would finally come out and the people of Canada would finally know what has taken place with regard to the Department of the Environment.
May 12, 1989

It is not good enough for us to have to identify the problems on the West Coast with regard to oil tanker spills and the damage to the environment. It is not good enough when we identify those subjects that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) rises in the House and praises his Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard). It is not good enough that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Jelinek) should rise in the House and state that his Department is quite clean, it has done its duty and carried out its process. That is not good enough. The Canadian people want more.
I have petitioned my constituency with regard to the environmental problem that we had in our riding. I received one of the biggest results in return with regard to the issue of burning those chemicals in an outdated burner. The Government had better start to address the environmental problems. It had better start now, and not only do it by attending conventions in Europe or in other countries, but start addressing the problems in Canada both with regard to the handling of dangerous chemicals, the effect it could have on our population, and with regard to the individual's right to live in a clean and healthy environment.
If the Government is going to act responsibly with its Environmental Protection Act, it should also include a section stating that when a company applies to carry out a project that could result in some environmental damage, and people want to attend a hearing to express their concerns, that that company should supply some funding in order that the people would be able to attend a hearing to express their concerns and conduct the research needed to address the problem that the company is trying to impose on them.
If the Government was acting responsibly with the environmental Act, it would place into the Act a provision that some funding would be made available in order that the respondents, the people who will be affected, will have an opportunity to receive funding to do the research to counteract what the company is saying, and to use that research in a responsible manner.
In this way we would all know that both the company and the residents who are living in that area will be protected and will feel that they have had their say, and that it has been conducted in a responsible manner with research required to be able to combat that type of a procedure. That is what must be done. It makes me mad

when I see the Minister of the Environment rise in the House and tell us what a great job his Department is doing.
I wrote to the Minister with regard to these problems. On March 9 I met with an official from the Minister's office to request that his Department test effluence from a pulp mill that was burning waste chemical products in an outdated burner. I had the samples with me and I was told that the samples could not be used, they would get their own, and that they would get back to me.
One month later, on April 3, I received a letter from the office of the Minister acknowledging that the meeting took place. I know that the meeting took place. The residents had waited with agonizing patience, and on May 4 again I wrote to the Minister and have yet to receive a reply. The Minister tells us what a great job his Department is doing. I told him where the problem was. I had the sample with me if he needed it, and to date I have not received an answer. The people in that riding stood up and fought to stop the project taking place. I am proud of the efforts of the citizens in the riding. However, I want to say to the Minister that he better start addressing the question, and he better start addressing it now. His Department had better start recognizing that it has a responsibility to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, a key question is whether the Government in fact is continuing to provide the resources necessary to ensure the health and safety of Canadians as well as giving them adequate services.
For two weeks we have been talking about how, where and with what effectiveness this Government uses the resources of Canadians to provide services to them. Throughout the last few months in looking at the kinds of cut-backs that have taken place in the Public Service, in the allocation of human resources to the provision of services mandated-may I remind the Government-by this Parliament to Canadians, we have identified that cut-backs have led to deterioration in air safety, in the

inspection and certification of carriers and pilots operating in this country while the number of people and planes flying has increased. We have identified that decreases in the numbers of inspectors and lack of adequate training has led to the deterioration in the protection of the food supply coming into Canada. We have identified, as substantiated by the Auditor General's report, that there is inadequate inspection to secure the health and safety of Canadians regarding pesticides and other food additives. Now we see the same thing occurring concerning the protection of Canadians from the entry of contaminated goods into our country.

This has resulted in the kind of confusion that led a Customs inspector, not two months ago, to let into Canada a shipment of meat in the same truck as, and unprotected from, hazardous chemicals. shipments coming in. That is what improved services with the same resources has meant to Canadians.
In air safety there has been a total shift from preventive regulation to enforcement after the fact, after accidents, deaths and injuries. If emphasis is being put on the inspection of fuels coming into Canada, from where will those resources be drawn? Just how much more can a reduced number of inspectors be asked to do at the border? They are being asked to implement zero tolerance with respect to drugs entering Canada. That is the priority for this year in the allocation of Customs officials. Now there is a new priority to inspect every tanker coming into Canada. This will add costs to the industry doing business in Canada by having them go hundreds of miles out of their way to go through another port because we do not have the resources to put inspectors at the most convenient border points.
We now have two high priorities because they are public issues. Where are the resources coming from? What kind of inspections will suffer? Will there be fewer inspections of food? To what extent was the inadequacy of resources responsible for the fact that when the Government of Canada was invited to participate with Ontario in the sweep inspection for hazardous wastes crossing the border it refused? The sole extent of its co-operation with the Government of Ontario was to allocate space at border points. Is that a positive response to a hazardous situation?
Just for the information of government Members, out of the 383 trucks that were stopped and tested during those four days of stepped up sweep, 18 charges were laid, not counting charges that will be laid out of 113 samples that were taken and were considered sufficiently questionable to have to be sent to laboratories for analysis.
The cut-back in resources is already having an effect that will be exacerbated by a new priority with no new resources. I would like to refer to a couple of situations that have come to my attention. At the Port of Niagara, there are line-ups of one to one and a half hours. Tourists and Canadians returning to Canada are being inconvenienced to that extent. Tourism operators at a number of border points are complaining about the effect this is having on tourism. Customs officers are being asked to work overtime and to work on a rotational shift that was abandoned in 1974 because it was considered inefficient and inhumane. Businesses in other areas are being affected.
There is a loss of revenue to Canada resulting from the lack of resources. More is being lost than anything that is being saved by reducing the number of people that are provided at borders for inspections.
Businesses are experiencing delays and difficulties in getting their goods released because there are not enough inspectors. Goods are being released without being inspected by commodity specialists and are therefore being undercharged on duty. The taxpayers are paying the cost of that.
We have heard a lot of talk this week about what Mr. Green had to say. One of the things he said was that what was required for inspectors at the border was training in the detection of hazardous wastes, and that is why I asked the Minister that question. Apparently there has been no contact with the union responsible for Customs and Excise inspectors at the borders, either in early April, when we were aware of additional inspection activity in the Province of Ontario, or since. There has been no attempt to solicit the co-operation or advice of the union on how an improved inspection process could be implemented.
Another concern arises out of this. For three years now, there has been a much more intensive investigation of fuel coming into Canada, not out of concern for the health and safety of Canadians or for the risks to the environment but out of concern for revenue. For three years, inspectors have been checking every shipment aside from those of major, well-known oil companies. Any independent truck coming into Canada has been tested to make sure that it is shipping home fuel and not diesel fuel when that is what it claims it is shipping. Those tests are still being carried out by border inspectors.
Have the border inspectors been warned that that testing may in fact be hazardous to their health? I can tell Hon. Members that they have not. Have we shown any concern for their health and safety at any time in the three-year period or at any time since whenever it was that Ministers of the Crown became aware of the potential risk? We have not. This is just one more incident that demonstrates that there is a very cavalier attitude toward the men and women who perform responsibilities on behalf of the people of Canada as directed and resourced by Parliament. We are not giving them sufficient resources or sufficient training. We are

not giving them adequate protection from the health risks involved in their occupations.
We are asking them to take on crackdowns on drugs, new regulations under the Free Trade Agreement, reduced inspections, increased inspections and changed working conditions. We are not giving them the resources to do the job and now we are asking them to take on one more priority. I challenge the Government, if it wants that to happen, to give the people the resources to do the job, give them the training to do the job, and protect their health and safety while they are working for the people of Canada.
This has been a long debate, but I think it has been a worth-while debate on behalf of the people of Canada. I think that the Opposition, I say in all modesty, has admirably done its job in holding the Government accountable in this debate.
